sentences.text: The name Perugyps combines the country of origin, Peru, with the Greek word for vulture.
The species name diazi honors Eusebio Díaz.
Specific features of the carpometacarpus — the main bone of the wing — identify Perugyps as a condor.
The anterior carpal fossa of Perugyps is less pneumatic than in modern birds.
The proximal symphysis of the Perugyps carpometacarpus is short, similar to the Andean condor.
The coronoid process of the Perugyps lower jaw is taller than in any living vulture.
The total length of the Perugyps lower jaw exceeds that of both modern condor species.
The area between the condyles on the Perugyps tarsometatarsus is deeper than in all living vultures and the extinct Geronogyps.
Perugyps is distinguished by a distal external trochlea placed lower than the middle trochlea, unlike extant cathartids.
Fossil evidence suggests Perugyps was approximately 7% larger than the Andean condor.
Degrange and colleagues estimate Perugyps was about 7% larger than the modern Andean condor and Vultur messii.
The genus Perugyps was described by Stucchi and Emslie in 2005.
Perugyps was described based on isolated fossil remains including wing parts, leg bones, and a lower jaw.
The fossils were discovered at the Montemar and Sacaco Sur localities in Peru's Pisco Formation.
The species was named by M. Stucchi and S. D. Emslie in 2005.
Perugyps diazi was found in the Pisco Formation in the Ica department of Peru.
Researchers speculate that Perugyps fed on marine mammal carcasses similar to modern vultures.
It is hypothesized that Perugyps also snatched chicks from local seabird colonies to supplement its diet.
Perugyps likely fed primarily on the diverse seabirds and marine mammals that shared its coastal habitat.
Researchers suggest Perugyps acted as a scavenger of marine mammal carcasses and may have also preyed on live bird chicks.
Perugyps diazi was a scavenger that lived on the beaches of modern-day Pisco alongside a high biodiversity of marine birds, whales, sharks, and giant penguins.
Stucchi and Emslie classified Perugyps as a condor based on three distinct characters of the carpometacarpus.
A 2015 study suggests Perugyps is closely associated with other South American condors like Gymnogyps howardae, Geronogyps, and the Andean condor.
The genus Perugyps was established by M. Stucchi and S. D. Emslie in 2005.
Perugyps is classified within the family Cathartidae.
The order of Perugyps is uncertain, with its family placed in Falconiformes, Accipitriformes, Ciconiiformes, or Cathartiformes.
Perugyps belongs to the subfamily Vulturinae.
Perugyps lived during the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene epochs.
Perugyps was found in the Pisco Formation of Peru.
Perugyps fossils were found in the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene Pisco Formation at the Montemar and Sacaco Sur localities.
The localities where Perugyps was found represent ancient coastal environments with protected beaches and reefs.
Perugyps lived between 7.246 and 5.333 million years ago during the Messinian age.
